newsitem.title: ANTARCTICA: FEATURE-Antarctic base gets serious about taking out trash.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Antarctic base gets serious about taking out trash.

text.p: Stung by international criticism that it was polluting the barren continent it was meant to study, the U.S. Antarctic programme has set tough rules on trash disposal that it hopes will give it a cleaner, greener image.

The rules, which take sanitation to a whole new dimension, include sorting and recycling of just about everything, a ban on items ranging from aerosol cans to house plants and strict rules on where you can urinate. "The idea is to reduce our footprint here. The whole programme has become very green," said Don Ferris, a former manager at the Palmer Station American scientific base at the foot of a glacier on Antarctica's Anvers Island.

Time to go to the dump? At Palmer Station it is about 900 miles (1,500 km) away in Punta Arenas, Chile, where all non-biodegradable wastes are shipped except for hazardous materials such as chemicals and petroleum products, which go all the way back to Texas.

Only sewage from the base's 50 or so people and food waste are not shipped out. Except for eggshells, these are macerated and then dispersed into the sea over a wide area, well away from wildlife breeding grounds, in line with rules set by the Antarctic Conservation Act passed by Congress.

Eggshells and other raw poultry products must be sterilised before they are chopped up because they carry avian bacteria that could trigger plagues among the area's many penguins, petrels and other birds if released untreated into the sea.

Things have changed since the late 1980s, when Palmer Station and a much larger U.S. base, McMurdo, used to anger Greenpeace and other environmental groups by burning garbage, leaving piles of abandoned machinery and pumping raw sewage into the ocean.

A Greenpeace report three years later also sharply criticised British, Argentine, Japanese and Chinese bases for leaving their garbage on the continent. At one Argentine base, for example, 30 years of trash had been accumulating at the bottom of a hill.

Most countries now claim they are cleaning up their acts and trying to reverse earlier damage. Workers at Palmer Station have been digging up ash and debris from the rubbish pit, removing 140 cubic yards (meters) of it last year, Ferris said. "They used to just heap up the trash and set fire to it," he said.

"The focus has changed to more emphasis on environmental protection. They've done a lot to clean up recently and I think NSF is proud of it," said Janet Phillips, manager at Palmer Station, referring to the National Science Foundation, which owns the base.

Strict rules on waste disposal extend to almost every aspect of daily life at the station. For example, scientists doing field work on nearby islands must go to the water's edge to relieve themselves. If they cannot make it that far, they are supposed to urinate into a bottle, according to rules written in Washington.

This is one rule that goes a little too far for some. "When you've got big trawlers hauling fish out by the tonne just north of the Antarctic, worrying about where people pee seems frankly a little silly," one scientist said.

All this attention to ecology is not just by choice. It is part of a milestone international protocol signed by the United States and 26 other countries in 1991 and setting environmental rules on the frozen continent for the next century.

The signers, ranging from Russia to Uruguay, have about 40 bases in Antarctica among them. The Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty orders them to keep adverse effects on air or water to a minimum. More importantly, it allows them to inspect each others' bases to ensure compliance.
It bans non-native plants and animals from the continent, so no more sled dogs. And in its most famous provision, it prohibits mining in Antarctica for at least 50 years.

The protocol was signed when memories were still fresh of perhaps the worst environmental incident in Antarctica, an oil spill caused when the Argentine ship Bahia Paraiso struck rocks near Palmer Station and capsized in 1989. Six hundred tonnes of fuel oil washed into the sea at penguin breeding season, soiling nesting grounds and killing chicks. The hull of the ship still lies on rocks, belly up and leaking small amounts of fuel.

"Until the Bahia Paraiso sank, the idea of an environmental disaster was seen as something remote, just a potential," said William Fraser of Montana State University, chief scientist at Palmer. "It made people suddenly aware of how fragile the environment is here, and that changed the whole thinking."
